title: Little v. Barreme (1804)
summary: A presidential instruction cannot authorize an officer to do what the statute does not permit, so a naval captain who seized a ship outside the terms of the Non-Intercourse Act was liable in damages despite obeying orders.
notes:
Key line: I acquiesce in that of my brethren, which is, that the instructions cannot change the nature of the transaction, or legalize an act which without those instructions would have been a plain trespass. (Chief Justice Marshall)

Citation: 6 U.S. (2 Cranch) 170 (1804).

sections.Parties: The appellants were George Little, captain of the United States frigate Boston, and the other captors who shared in the seizure. The appellees were Barreme and the other owners of the Danish brigantine Flying Fish, who claimed the vessel and her cargo. The seizure took place during the undeclared naval conflict with France under the Non-Intercourse Act of February 9, 1799. Dexter argued for the captors; Martin and Mason argued for the claimants. The instructions under which Captain Little acted had been issued by the Secretary of the Navy on March 12, 1799 at the command of President Adams.
sections.Material Facts: Section 1 of the Act of February 9, 1799 forbade any vessel owned or employed by residents of the United States to proceed to any French port. Section 5 authorized the President to instruct commanders of armed vessels to stop and examine any ship of the United States on the high seas suspected of trading with France and, if she appeared to be bound or sailing to a French port, to seize her and send her to the nearest American port. The Secretary of the Navy's instructions of March 12, 1799 told commanders to treat section 5 as part of their orders but went further, directing them to seize vessels bound to or from French ports. On December 2, 1799, the Flying Fish, a Danish vessel carrying Danish and neutral property, sailing from Jeremie, a French port on Hispaniola, to St. Thomas, was captured by the Boston and the General Greene and taken to Boston.
sections.Procedural History: The captors libeled the vessel in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts. The District Judge ordered the vessel and cargo restored to the claimants as neutral property but refused to award damages, finding probable cause to suspect the ship was American. The claimants appealed to the Circuit Court, which reversed on the question of damages because the Flying Fish had been sailing from, not to, a French port and so was not liable to capture even had she been American; it awarded damages against Captain Little. The captors appealed to the Supreme Court. The case was argued at the December 1801 term and decided on February 27, 1804. The Court affirmed the decree with costs. Chief Justice Marshall delivered the opinion of the Court.
sections.Issue: Did the President's instructions, which directed naval commanders to seize American vessels sailing to or from French ports, protect Captain Little from liability in damages for seizing a vessel sailing from a French port, when the Act of Congress authorized seizure only of vessels bound to French ports? A second question was whether the probable cause to suspect the Flying Fish of being American, which the trial judge found, would excuse the seizure and detention of what proved to be a neutral Danish vessel and whether the captors were therefore answerable in damages.
sections.Holding: No. The instructions cannot change the nature of the transaction or legalize an act that would otherwise be a plain trespass. Congress in the fifth section prescribed the manner of executing the law, limiting seizures on the high seas to American vessels bound to French ports, and the President could not enlarge that authority by instruction. Because the Flying Fish was sailing from a French port, the seizure would have been unauthorized even had she been American, so it is unnecessary to decide whether probable cause to suspect her American character would have excused Captain Little; she was in fact Danish, and the captors are liable. The decree of the Circuit Court awarding damages is affirmed with costs.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Marshall first examined the statute. Congress plainly wished to cut off all commerce between American vessels and France, but in section 5 it chose to authorize seizure on the high seas only of vessels bound to French ports. The Executive read the Act more broadly and instructed commanders to seize vessels sailing from French ports as well, a construction Marshall thought better suited to the law's object but one Congress had not adopted. Had Congress given no direction about execution, the President's general duty and his command of the navy might have justified the seizure of any offending vessel, but Congress prescribed the manner in which the law was to be carried into execution and thereby excluded seizure of vessels coming from French ports. Marshall candidly recorded his own first impression: that a military officer obeying the orders of his superior should be shielded from damages for an act he could not lawfully refuse. He reported that he had been convinced he was mistaken and acquiesced in the view of his brethren that instructions cannot alter the legal character of the act or legalize a trespass. Because the seizure was unauthorized on any view of the vessel's nationality, the Court did not reach the probable cause question, which would matter only if the seizure of an American vessel had been lawful. The Danish character of the ship and cargo made the captors trespassers liable in damages.

topics.lrs-o-ministerial-duties: Presidential instruction did not protect an officer who undertook a seizure outside Congress’s statutory limits.
topics.lrs-o-executive-orders: Presidential instructions could not authorize a seizure beyond what Congress permitted, the classic limit on executive directives.

learning.separateOpinions: None. Chief Justice Marshall delivered the opinion for a unanimous Court.
